Just a note on what's going on under the hood.

We set things like step sizes to expect a certain amount of
rejection. As long as it doesn't lead to too strong a correlation
in the output traceplots, it's OK in the sense that the posterior
samples are still drawn properly.

The non-positive definite matrices typically arise from arithmetic
issues in either underflow/overflow, non-transitivity of
addition [ (a + b) + c is not necessarily the same as a + (b + c)
in floating point ], and too large a step size in the Hamiltonian
dynamics simulation (which is intentional to get a good balance
between rejection and movement, just as in Metropolis sampling).

- Bob

Right.

I don't think we can just Cholesky factor a correlation matrix,
because we won't be accounting for the Jacobian.  It really does
require us to have a correlation Cholesky factor type.

I just filed an issue to remove it from the function signatures for
2.0.

The only situation in which it makes sense to use currently is:

parameters {
  corr_matrix[K] Sigma;
}
model {
  matrix[K,K] L;
  L <- cholesky_decompose(Sigma);
  L ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(eta); // implies: lkj_cor(eta) prior on Sigma
  // use L for some other calculation
}

This is a tiny bit faster (but more confusing) than just doing

Sigma ~ lkj_corr(eta);

because lkj_corr() internally calculates the Cholesky factor of Sigma in order to evaluate the determinant of Sigma. Worse, lkj_corr() also validates whether Sigma is, in fact, (numerically) positive definite, so it actually takes the Cholesky factorization twice.

But I don't know if avoiding that redundant calculation is worth the confusion, particularly if we soon add (to the confusion with) the density on L such that L * L' is a correlation matrix that is distributed LKJ with shape eta.

Ben

The reason lkj_corr_choleksy() doesn't throw warnings and should be somewhat faster than lkj_corr() is that lkj_corr() checks whether its argument is in fact a correlation matrix (symmetric, unit diagonal, positive definite) whereas lkj_corr_cholesky() doesn't check anything, not even that its argument is lower-triangular. This is right mathematically, but an explicit
loop should be faster in Stan because you don't have
to create the diagonal matrix and do all the needless
multiplications by 1.

So that'd be:

Sigma[1,1] <- sigma[1] * sigma[1] * R[1,1];
Sigma[2,2] <- sigma[2] * sigma[2] * R[2,2];
Sigma[1,2] <- sigma[1] * sigma[2] * R[1,2];
Sigma[2,1] <- Sigma[1,2];

The last step is to cut down on allocations of auto-diff variables.
It's valid because R and Sigma are symmetric. In general, the
loop for size K, arranged to exploit memory locality in column-major
matrix storage would be:

for (n in 1:K)
for (m in 1:n)
Sigma[m,n] <- sigma[m] * sigma[n] * R[m,n];
for (n in 1:K)
for (m in (n+1):K)
Sigma[m,n] <- Sigma[n,m];

It'd be even hair faster if you split the diagonal out and
use the square() function [may not be available until 2.0],
but the above should be sufficient.

If I'm not mistaken, it might be even better to rescale
at the Cholesky factor level --- I'm too lazy to try

There's a pretty thorough description of the transforms we use in
the chapter near the end of the manual on variable transforms.
It's easiest to understand in the 1D case, especially if you draw
out some examples and think about probability masses of intervals.
(Beyond 1D, it's volume, which is why you see the determinant term.)
> Are there any wrong manual constructions in model 2 or 3?

(2) is fine. You can always transform a parameter and use it
on the right-side as an argument to a distribution. The problem
is when you do it on the left side, as in:

parameters {
real<lower=0> tau;
...
transformed parameters {
real<lower=0> sigma;
...
model {
sigma <- 1 / sqrt(tau);
tau ~ gamma(alpha,beta);
y ~ normal(mu, sigma);

It doesn't matter if sigma is a transformed parameter or declared
as a local variable, or just used implicitly through its
expression, as in:

y ~ normal(mu, 1 / sqrt(tau));

What you can't do without the Jacobian adjustment is go the other way
around and sample something that's been transformed:

parameters {
real<lower=0> sigma;
...
transformed parameters {
real<lower=0> tau;
model {
tau <- 1 / (sigma * sigma);
tau ~ gamma(alpha, beta);
y ~ normal(mu,sigma);

You need to account for the Jacobian of the transform, which in
the 1D case is just the absolute derivative. And we work on
the log scale, so there's a log on the outside.
In this case, the transform is 1 / (sigma * sigma), which
is just sigma^{-2}. The adjustment needed is then:

log | d/d.sigma sigma^{-2} |

= log | -2 sigma^{-3} |

= log 2 sigma^{-3}

= log 2 + log sigma^{-3}

= log 2 - 3 * log sigma

We're working on a log scale, so you'd need to add to the model:

lp__ <- lp__ + log(2) - 3 * log(sigma);

And you can drop the log(2) in Stan, because we only need the
log probability defined up to an additive constant.

Your model (3) is conceptually wrong because you're sampling a transformed Cholesky
factor L without the change-of-variables adjustment. But,
you won't see it in this example's output because your choice of prior:

L ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(1.0);

This is just uniform on L, which means it's effectively a no-op in Stan.
You're left with the implicit uniform distribution on R that is implicit
in its declaration as a correlation matrix.

By the way, this is true of the other models, too. Correlation matrices
are bounded to (-1,1), so declaring a variable as a correlation matrix
gives it a proper uniform prior over correlation matrices. You should
read Ben's paper on visualizing covariance priors to see what the implications
are.

Maybe I should put this example in the manual under the transforms
section. After getting Ben to verify that it's right!

- Bob

Three models:
a) same data, parameters, and transformed parameters block:

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  vector[2] y[N];
}
parameters {
  vector[2] mu;
  vector<lower=0>[2] sigma;

b) three model blocks:

model {                    // 1 : LKJ
  R ~ lkj_corr(1.0);
  for (n in 1:N)
    y[n] ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma);
}

model {                    // 2 : LKJ + Cholesky
  matrix[2,2] L;
  R ~ lkj_corr(1.0);
  L <- cholesky_decompose(R);
  for (n in 1:N)
    y[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, D * L);
}

Explicitly doing

R ~ lkj_corr(1.0)

is just a waste of time. The 1.0 implies the density is a constant, so no matter the value of the off-diagoals of R, the posterior is the same. However, lkj_corr() will check whether R is in fact a correlation matrix, which is very expensive at least for large K. And you may get a few messages that say a proposal was rejected because R was not (numerically) positive definite. The modeler knows that R is a correlation matrix but Stan doesn't.

And model 2 is not really much different than model 1. Basically, multi_normal(mu, Sigma) is doing a Cholesky factorization of Sigma. The main difference is again that Stan checks whether Sigma is in fact a covariance matrix, which is already known by the modeler.

model {                    // 3 : lkj_corr_cholesky
  matrix[2,2] L;
  L <- cholesky_decompose(R);
  L ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(1.0);
  for (n in 1:N)
    y[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, D * L);
}

This is right, but I would honestly rather it not be included as an example. The lkj_corr_cholesky function is going to be deprecated soon, or possibly reincarnated as the density such that L * L' is distributed LKJ(eta).

Ben: "It would also yield the wrong answer if you manually constructed an L such that L * L' is a correlation matrix unless you also manually made the Jacobian correction." I'm aware of the Jacobian of the transformation of random variables, and there are several examples in (probability textbooks, and in) the manual, but I can't even imagine what you are speaking of. I mean that I'd only be able to "construct" such an L by L <- cholesky_decompose(R). But I'm just a learner.
Are there any wrong manual constructions in model 2 or 3?

They aren't wrong. According to the LKJ paper,

f(R|eta) \propto det(R)^(eta - 1)

so if you do a change-of-variables

abs(det(J)) * det(L)^(2 * eta - 2)

where J is the Jacobian of the transformation from the lower-triangular elements of L to the lower-triangular elements of R. J is lower-triangular, so its determinant is relatively easy to calculate (and only involves the diagonal elements of L), but is nevertheless confusing and risky for a user to do in a model block.

After 2.0 gets released, we want to 1) Introduce the Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix as a primitive data type that users can declare in the parameters block and 2) introduce a (log) density function that does the (log of) the preceding automatically in an optimized way. That should make an example 4 be much faster than your three examples because you avoid having to calculate any Cholesky factors from square matrices which is O(K^3) and relies entirely on Stan's auto-diff capabilities.

Ben

Right.
> b) sampling: K(K-1)/2 values are sampled from their distributions (according to that probability function);

This isn't quite how things work. Stan just defines a log probability
density and samples from that.

The density is defined, by default, to be uniform on the support of
all of the parameters (support being defined by the constraints).

So if you declare a correlation matrix Omega, it's implicitly defining
a uniform distribution

p(Omega) propto constant

> c) inverse transform: those values are used to build a correlation matrix by the LKJ transform and the Jacobian of the
> inverse transform.

The above, p(Omega) propto constant, arises as a result of adjusting
for the Jacobian. If we just let everything be uniform on the (K choose 2)
basis, it wouldn't be uniform on the covariance matrix Omega.

> If those K(K-1)/2 values are sampled from a uniform distribution, it is as if the correlation matrix was sampled from a
> uniform distribution on KxK correlation matrices.

The (K choose 2) vals are what the underlying HMC sampler uses.
They're never sampled uniformly, but only sampled after the
transform. So if y_1 ... y_{K choose 2} is the basis,
then

Omega = inverse_transform(y)

where the transform is defined from Omega to y.

The trick is when you add another sampling statement, like:

Omega ~ lkj_corr(2.0);

then that gets multiplied into the total probability, so
now

p(Omega) propto constant * lkj_corr(Omega|2.0)

- Bob
